summary: This informational RFC discusses queuing algorithms and marking or dropping algorithms. While they may be implemented together, it argues that specifications, measurements and comparisons should treat them separately and show how each contributes to system behavior.

plainLanguage.summary: A line at a shop has two choices: who goes next and who gets turned away. This says we should judge those two choices separately.

subtitle: Separating queuing algorithms from marking and dropping to understand network behavior

tldr.problem: Network implementations couple queuing algorithms (which decide packet order and scheduling) with marking/dropping algorithms (which signal congestion). This makes it hard to measure which algorithm is responsible for observed behavior.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC argues that these should be treated as separate, sequential stages: queuing happens first, then marking/dropping, then transmission. Different combinations produce different signals to senders.
tldr.outcome: Clearer specifications, better measurements, and fairer comparisons of queuing and AQM algorithms—each can be evaluated for what it actually does.

today: RFC 7806 is an Informational RFC presenting an educational framework for understanding packet queuing and congestion management. It has not been obsoleted and informs the design of active queue management systems in modern networks.

sections.title: The Case for Separating Concerns
sections.content:
Active Queue Management (AQM) combines two types of algorithms. Queuing algorithms decide the order packets are forwarded and which flows get priority. Marking/dropping algorithms signal congestion by marking packets with Explicit Congestion Notification (ECN) or dropping them, rather than waiting for timeout-based loss.

The RFC notes that while these algorithms are often implemented together, they should be specified, measured, and compared separately. Different combinations send different signals to applications: ack clocking from the queue itself, early congestion signals from the AQM, and defensive loss when buffers overflow. Understanding each signal's source helps operators and researchers design better systems.
sections.plainLanguage: A queue and a bouncer do different jobs. The queue orders people; the bouncer turns away the overflow. It helps to grade them separately.

sections.title: Fair Queuing and Generalized Processor Sharing
sections.content:
The RFC explores the history of fair queuing, which tries to give every flow a fair share of bandwidth. The ideal model is Generalized Processor Sharing (GPS), which imagines serving each flow in parallel at its allocated rate. Real packet networks cannot do this—packets are indivisible—so many implementations approximate GPS.

Key choices in fair queuing include: whether to measure in packets or bytes, how to define a flow (source address, destination, TCP session, customer), and what transmission quantum to use. Different choices yield different fairness properties. The RFC also distinguishes work-conserving queues, which keep transmitting while data is available, from non-work-conserving ones, which may pause to enforce rate limits.
sections.plainLanguage: Fair queuing tries to give every flow equal time. Real networks have different ways to do this depending on what counts as a flow and whether you send in packets or bytes.

sections.title: Queuing Algorithms: Implementation Approaches
sections.content:
The RFC outlines several families of queuing algorithms. Round-robin queues cycle through subqueues for each flow, sending a quantum of data from each in turn. Calendar queue models schedule data for transmission at future times or sequences, useful for time-based rate limits. Stochastic Fairness Queuing (SFQ) hashes packets to random subqueues to approximate fair queuing without per-flow state. Deficit Round Robin (DRR) extends round-robin to handle variable-length packets by tracking a quantum deficit per flow.

Virtual Clock is a non-work-conserving algorithm that schedules each packet to a future time interval based on the flow's rate. If not enough time has elapsed, the packet waits. These approaches trade memory, CPU, and fairness properties against each other.
sections.plainLanguage: Different ways to organize a line: go around the room once per cycle, assign time slots in a calendar, randomly hash people to lanes, or schedule people to exact times.

sections.title: Marking and Dropping Algorithms
sections.content:
Three common marking/dropping approaches are described. Tail drop marks or drops only when the queue overflows, providing no early signal. CoDel marks or drops when packets have been delayed beyond a threshold, signaling congestion based on queueing delay. RED and PIE drop randomly when the queue reaches a certain depth, aiming to limit average delay.

These algorithms can be combined with any queuing algorithm. A FIFO+CoDel system sends four signals: ack clocking from the queue, early marking from CoDel, intentional loss when marking fails, and defensive drop on overflow. The RFC argues this separation helps explain the system's behavior more clearly than treating the pair as a single black box.
sections.plainLanguage: Different ways to say the line is too long: turn people away only when full, turn them away when they've waited too long, or turn them away randomly before they're too frustrated.

sections.title: Implications for Specification and Measurement
sections.content:
The RFC concludes that queuing and marking/dropping should be specified and measured separately. Queuing algorithms manage flow scheduling and fairness; marking/dropping algorithms signal congestion. Each contributes different effects: scheduling provides flow isolation, ack clocking provides rate feedback, AQM provides early signals, and defensive drop protects the network.

Implementations should be able to couple them in various ways—a FIFO queue with CoDel, an SFQ queue with RED, a Virtual Clock with PIE, or others. Each combination is valid and might suit different deployments. Measuring and comparing them separately, rather than as monolithic systems, leads to clearer results and better understanding of what works and why.
sections.plainLanguage: Grade the queuing and the dropping separately. The best queuing plus the best dropping might not make the best system—it depends on what you're trying to achieve.

left.title: Work-conserving
left.desc: Keep forwarding data at line rate while queue is not empty.

right.title: Non-work-conserving
right.desc: Stop and wait to enforce an upper-bound rate, even if queue has data.
